# The Android Who Saved Soul: Janelle Monáe’s Sci-Fi Music Revolution

By **Greg LaRose**, CNN
April 15, 2009 

**(CNN) —** In a pop music landscape currently dominated by auto-tuned club anthems and hyper-sexualized image craft, Janelle Monáe stands out like a time traveler from the 28th century. 

Dressed in her trademark, pristine black-and-white tuxedo, her hair sculpted into a gravity-defying pompadour, the 23-year-old singer-songwriter looks less like a typical R&B starlet and more like a character straight out of a classic sci-fi film. 

And that is precisely the point.

Over the past year, Monáe has become one of the music industry's most talked-about rising stars, captivating critics and fans alike with her explosive stage presence, genre-bending music, and an elaborate narrative concept centered around her android alter ego, Cindi Mayweather.

### A Voice for the 'Other'

Monáe’s musical story began taking the world by storm with her 2007 EP, *Metropolis: Suite I (The Chase)*. The concept album introduces listeners to Cindi Mayweather, an android living in the year 2719 who falls in love with a human and is sentenced to "dismantling" for breaking the law. 

While a sci-fi rock opera about a love-struck robot might seem like a hard sell for mainstream radio, Monáe insists the storyline is a deeply personal metaphor for modern societal struggles.

"The android represents the 'Other' in our society," Monáe tells CNN. "Whether you're talking about race, sexual orientation, or religion, the android is symbolic of anyone who feels marginalized, silenced, or pushed to the fringes. Cindi is a mediator between the oppressed and the oppressors."

Musically, Monáe’s sound is impossible to box into a single genre. Her songs effortlessly blend 1960s Motown soul, punk rock, cabaret, jazz, and futuristic orchestral arrangements. On her breakout single "Many Moons"—which earned a Grammy nomination earlier this year for Best Urban/Alternative Performance—she raps, sings, and belts over a frantic, uptempo beat that sounds like James Brown jamming with Prince in the year 3000.

### From Kansas to Metropolis

Monáe’s path to the future began in Kansas City, Kansas, where she grew up singing in church and dreaming of performing. Seeking a creative environment where she could fully express her vision, she moved to Atlanta, Georgia, where she co-founded the Wondaland Arts Society—an artistic collective dedicated to nurturing original, avant-garde talent.

Her big break came when Outkast’s Big Boi caught her performing at an Atlanta open-mic night. Impressed by her energy, he featured her on Outkast's 2006 soundtrack album *Idlewild*. Shortly after, hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs heard *Metropolis* and was so stunned that he signed her directly to Bad Boy Records in late 2007.

"She is one of the most important artists of our time," Combs said in a recent press event. "When I saw her, I knew I was looking at the future. She doesn't follow trends; she sets her own path."

Combs’ endorsement gave Monáe a major distribution platform while allowing her complete creative freedom—a rarity for a new artist in the modern music business.

### The Tuxedo Revolution

Beyond her music, Monáe is making a bold statement with her wardrobe. In an era where female artists are often pressured to strip down to sell records, Monáe refuses to wear anything other than a tailored black-and-white suit.

"I wear a tuxedo because it’s my uniform," Monáe explains. "It pays homage to my parents. My mother was a janitor and my father was a trash collector, and they wore uniforms every single day to give me a chance at a better life. When I put this on, it reminds me that I have work to do. It keeps the focus on my music and my message, not on my body."

### Looking to the Future

The strategy is paying off. Having spent recent months opening for high-profile acts like No Doubt and Katy Perry, Monáe is proving that mainstream audiences are hungry for substance alongside spectacle. 

Later this year, she plans to release her highly anticipated full-length debut album, tentatively titled *The ArchAndroid*, which promises to continue the saga of Cindi Mayweather.

For Monáe, the mission is simple: to inspire people to break free from conformity.

"I want to make music that wakes people up," Monáe says with a smile. "We’re living in a time where people are afraid to be different. I’m just trying to show them that it's okay to be an android."
